Real-time systems and Embedded systems schedulability analysis

div.p: Component-based design is important for the design of complex embedded software. By properly defining component interfaces, new components can be formed by composing existing components. A newly formed component may be further composed of other components. One of the key requirements for guaranteeing the compositionality of components in real-time systems is that the composite model must be consistent with, and indistinguishable from, the interface of a primitive component so that all real-time requirements are met. In addition to being used widely for schedulability analysis on different techniques such as earliest deadline first (EDF) and rate monotonic (RM), supply-demand functions have been applied to perform compositional schedulability analysis with periodic resource models. However, supply-demand function analysis for compositional schedules has only been done for hard real-time systems guarantees. This work analyzes overloads in embedded real-time control systems with soft deadlines and the analysis helps to build a compositional system that can tolerate delays. This paper also associates the schedulability analysis with a control application using a rapid prototype implementation.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Compositionality is a way to convert multiple independent timing requirements of different components of a system into a single real-time system timing requirement. Satisfying timing requirements together with logical correctness can make a real-time system predictable, guaranteeing that it will operate correctly when deployed. Embedded real-time control systems often consist of smaller modules, which interact with each other. Such a structure makes embedded systems scalable because of the component oriented design. This approach provides a means for composing multiple components of a system, enabling the reduction of a complex design problem into multiple simpler design problems. Since, in practice, it is often preferable to work at higher levels of abstraction by reusing already verified components, it is often argued that as the system complexity increases, compositionality analysis towards component-oriented designs is the only way to reach design productivity.

Aiming at building a flexible compositional framework requires meeting demands of different types of real-time systems co-existing together. Fundamental to such a framework is the challenge of computing the optimal schedule from the collective resource, i.e., timing requirements for different types of guarantees. Seamless transition between guarantees provides flexibility in using the system effectively for different types of requirements, from soft realtime systems to hard real-time systems and vice-versa.

In the case of soft deadlines, the timing requirements are flexible and application dependent. An industrial control system is an example of a real-time system which can have varieties of timing requirements depending upon the specifications and types of systems to be controlled. Quality of Service (QoS) in such a system refers to different classes of timing guarantees for completing tasks. Services differentiated using timing requirements motivate the composition of real-time tasks according to soft deadlines.

The purpose of scheduling is to allocate resources according to different scheduling policies [7] such as earliest deadline first (EDF) and rate monotonic scheduling (RM). To support compositional scheduling, Shin and Lee [11] propose a scheduling interface model I(S, D), where S represents the resource supply that the system can provide and D represents the resource demand that the system requires. The composed scheduling model which has been analyzed regarding timing supply and demand for hard realtime systems is computed from the independent scheduling models having timing guarantees that satisfy those of the composed model.

Compositionality analysis with soft deadlines enables engineers to build a flexible system infrastructure. This also opens the door to the use of compositionality in mixed-critical systems because of the co-existing applications with different timing requirements. Converting mixed-timing requirements into single timing requirements creates the challenge of devising a demand function and supply function, both of which are flexible. Rather being strictly less than or equal to the supply function value, a demand function value will be able to relax this constraint if the system permits dropping some samples of the transmission. However, the amount that the demand function exceeds the supply function is bounded, which depends on the tolerance of the dropping rates of inter-arrival samples.

In real-time systems, overload is categorized into two types: transient and permanent. A transient overload can occur because of the excess demand of the execution time of tasks. This type of overload can occur for the simultaneous arrival of asynchronous events. If the utilization of the processor exceeds one, then a permanent overload is said to occur in periodic systems. This could happen for a number of reasons such as activation of a new periodic task and increase the activation rate of some tasks.

Another term related to overload is called overrun that occurs when a task executes more than expected. This situation may occur for two reasons: (1) jobs arrive more frequently than expected, or (2) computation time exceeds their expected value. The difference between overload and overrun is that the latter one is related to a single job whereas the overload is related to the processor. A single task overrun may not necessarily mean causing an overload in the system.

Schedulability is one of the key factors in compositionality analysis. If a certain configuration of compositional task sets is unschedulable, then the scheduler will try to find another configuration of compositional task sets to ensure that the system will work according to the specifications. Executables having unschedulable task sets are unsafe to operate for real-time systems. A number of real-time scheduling algorithms exist such as fixed priority scheduling, time-triggered scheduling, and earliest deadline first algorithm. In general, a scheduling algorithm that might be best suited for some applications might be less well suited for other application. To facilitate a high degree of flexibility and separation of concerns, different components of the system use different scheduling algorithms to achieve good performance and maximum resource utilization.
Apart from the previous work on compositionality analysis, this work contributes the following:
• analysis of compositionality for EDF-scheduled periodic systems that can handle overloads.

• analysis of the supply and demand bound functions for soft real-time systems and propose a new method for calculating the difference between resource and workload utilization at any time for compositional real-time control systems.
• discussion on the applicability of proposed schedulability analysis in compositional real-time control systems that can tolerate bounded delays.

The remainder of this paper is structure as follows: Section 2 presents some related work on compositionality analysis. Section 3 addresses the problem statement. In Section 4, the system model is presented. The characterization on the area of supply and demand bound functions is shown in Section 5 and characterize the overload and recovery areas in Section 6. Section 7 discusses the schedulability analysis for control systems using supply and demand bound areas. Section 8 shows the experimental results, and Section 9 concludes the paper.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: Shin and Lee [11] propose a compositional real-time scheduling framework for real-time systems which can be used to establish global (system level) timing properties by composing individual timing properties. The authors present schedulability conditions for the standard Liu and Layland periodic resource task model and propose periodic resource model under EDF and RM scheduling that allows composing multiple timing requirements into a single timing requirement. In another related work [10], the authors analyze compositional schedulability of a bounded delay resource partition model. Deducing a single timing requirement out of multiple timing properties creates some new challenges which have been solved in some subsequent works [9,11]. As a variant of the system model [10], Shin et al. also propose algorithms that define optimal interfaces for the subsystems which may share resources. Integrating subsystems into a system having optimal interfaces motivates the development of an adaptive and reconfigurable system. Wandeler and Thiele [12] propose a compositional analysis framework that uses real-time interfaces. Real-time interfaces are based on assume/guarantee (A/G) interfaces [12].

An important property of compositionality analysis that has drawn attention to the research community is optimization. Easwaran et al. [1] show that selecting a particular resource model that minimizes the collective resource requirements, facilitate systems to change components on the fly. Lee et al. propose an optimization framework for maximizing the quality of service (QoS) under K random failures on schedulability. The authors use Langarian duality [4] for distributed computation that results in optimal solutions.

An interesting way to narrow down the schedulability problem is the use of a resource reservation scheme [6]. The basic idea is that a fraction of the available processor bandwidth is reserved for each task which is assigned a server. If the task tries to use more than it has been assigned, the computation time will be slowed down. Therefore, the problem of schedulability analysis can be reduced to the problem of adaptation of the computation time. Lipari and Baruah in [5] presented schedulability conditions for EDF and RM scheduling that assume a priori knowledge of all task deadlines. Mok and Feng present a hierarchical partitioning methodology of a computational resource in [8], which describes the possibility of composing schedules at arbitrary levels of the hierarchy.

div.head: PROBLEM STATEMENT
div.p: Compositionality has been analyzed for hard real-time systems which may further be extended for soft real-time systems. Compositionality is possible when the original set of timing interfaces can accommodate an additional timing interface with sufficient capacity of allowing new tasks. An important aspect of compositionality analysis is the schedulability analysis of a composed system.

Supply and demand bound functions have been used for schedulability analysis under a particular scheduling model such as EDF and RM. A system will be schedulable if the resource supply (sbf) is no less than the workload demand (dbf) at any time. However, the condition sbf (t) ≥ dbf (t) can be relaxed for soft real-time systems. For a compositional soft real-time system, the analysis can be done for each level of composition. The relaxation of demand can be referred as overloads in the system that can occur temporarily.

An overload is said to occur when the demand of the execution tasks exceeds the resource supply. This might occur because of arriving more tasks than expected or because computation time of a task exceeds it's expected value. On the other hand, if an overload occurs and a computational task cannot be completed, then it will be able to use the computational resources that will be available later. Areas under sbf (t) and dbf (t) can characterize the overload situation and the recovery of the overload. Therefore, a mathematical model is devised to calculate the overload and recovery area to schedule tasks at time t to compensate the excess demand at time t ′ < t. The largest delay for which the overload area is compensated by recovery area is the inherent worst-case delay for completing tasks.

div.head: SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: This work assumes a compositional system that has multiple components. Each component has a periodic resource model and a periodic workload. The periodic resource specification for a component turns into a periodic workload when getting composed into a hierarchical compositional system.

A periodic resource model indicates the resource replenishment in each period. Given a periodic resource model R(λ, θ), tasks can be allocated for θ time units in λ units of time. A workload consists of a single task or multiple tasks. A task is a fundamental element of the system model which is activated multiple times by external or internal events. A task Ti is characterized by a tuple (pi, ei) where pi is the period and ei is the execution time. A number of tasks constitute a cycle which repeatedly executes in a defined sequence.

In this paper, the schedulability analysis is based on EDF. Therefore, the tasks in the workload are scheduled under EDF. However, the concept can easily be extended to other type of scheduling schemes such as RM scheduling.

div.head: ANALYZING OVERLOADS
div.p: A compositional system is formed using several smaller components and each component can experience or tolerate a fixed amount of overloads. Therefore, it is required to analyze overloads in each of the individual components that are merged to form a compositional system. Analyzing overloads for each of the components refers to identifying the metric for characterization of an overload.

div.head: ANALYZING RECOVERY
div.p: A recovery of an overload indicates that the system can tolerate the effects of an overload. An overload can occur for different reasons such as changes in the environment, faults of peripheral devices, or system exceptions. This paper discusses how overloads can be analyzed, recovered, and check whether the system is still schedulable under certain overloads. It is necessary to recover from overloads for each of the components of a compositional system.

The overload area is the total area covered outside the supply demand function by the demand bound function in each hyperperiod. This area is the summation of all overloads calculated in between the successive intersections of the supply bound and demand bound curves when the tasks' demand is greater than the resource supply. If computational resources are available at some time t and do not get used, it is not required to get them back again because they are gone forever. On the other hand, if a computational task does not have sufficient resources at time t, it can sit around and wait for computational resources to become available later. Therefore, the measurement of areas starts when sbf first becomes less than the dbf, because this is the point at which overloads start accumulating (i.e., overload area increases), which must be compensated by excess resources later.

div.head: OVERLOADS AND ITS RECOVERY IN COMPOSITIONAL EMBEDDED REAL-TIME CONTROL SYSTEMS
div.p: The overloads and its recovery in compositional embedded realtime systems can be associated to maintaining stability. The stability of a control component can be guaranteed even in the presence of timing violations of some control messages i.e., tasks [2]. A timing violation can be characterized as an overload condition in our case. If the system remains still schedulable after the timing violations, then the recovery area is big enough to schedule the tasks that have missed their deadlines. Characterizing such area thus helps us identifying the worst case delay that the task that has missed the deadline can be rescheduled within the recovery area.

div.head: Simulation Study
div.p: A simulation is performed to see what parameters in the periodic resource model can increase the chance of having overloads. It is also shown that how can an increasing number of tasks can increase the probability of having overloads. The experiments show that the overestimation is acceptable.

Lets consider a scheduling model M (W, R(5, 3), EDF ) that has five tasks in the workload, W = {T1(7, 3), T2(21, 1), T3(42, 2), T4(63, 1), T5(84, 2)}. This model is schedulable because ∀t: sbf(t) ≥ dbf(W, t, EDF ) which is shown in Figure 6. The simulations have been performed for four variations in the workload which are done by: (1) increasing the execution time of the tasks (case 1), (2) decreasing the periodicity of tasks (case 2), (3) decreasing the periodic resource execution time (case 3), and (4) increasing the resource period (case 4).

Figure 7 shows the increase of overload due to the increase of the execution time (see Figure 7(a)) of tasks, the decrease of the tasks period (see Figure 7(b)), the decrease of the periodic execution time (Figure 7(c)), and the increase of the resource period (see Figure 7(d)). Since the overload increases, the system more likely becomes non-schedulable. In all cases, two situations of overloads are shown. First, the overload is recoverable because the area of supply bound function is greater than the area of demand bound function. Second, the overload is irrecoverable because the area of supply bound function is smaller than the area of demand bound function. The workload increase can be done by adding tasks. After a single task (48, 3) is added to the workload, it is found that the overload is recoverable because the area of supply bound function is greater than the area of demand bound function. Then three tasks ((14, 3),(28, 2),(48, 3)) are added to the workload and it is found that the overload is irrecoverable because the area of supply bound function is smaller than the area of demand bound function. Therefore, with the increase of the number of tasks in the system, the overload increases and this increases the likelihood of the system becoming non-schedulable (see Figure 8). The addition of new tasks refers to the compositionality of the system.

div.head: Case Study
div.p: The experimental evaluation also contains a rapid prototype implementation of a case study on analyzing overloads in a control application. The control application stabilizes a double inverted pendulum (DIP). The DIP setup contains a hard real-time operating system QNX which is connected to the inverted pendulum for controlling the stability. To model the DIP application, Quanser rapid prototype environment QUARC is used as a control software that has been used for running several real-time experiments such as unmanned aerial vehicles, unmanned ground vehicles, and mobile robots [3].

The case study considers both computation and communication faults, and these are simulated using poisson distribution. The fault frequency ranges from low to high depending upon the poisson distribution factor lambda. In our experiments, the larger the value lambda the higher the number of faults. In our case when a fault occurs, the feedback input to the controller is set to zero. Table 1 shows the mean time to stabilize the inverted pendulum and the standard deviation of the calculation. Five different experiments were performed and the same experiment was run for three times. Among these different configurations of the system, the worst-case time required to stabilize the system is 8.313 sec, and the standard deviation is 2.460 sec. The delay follows the bound as specified in Equation 9. Therefore, the overloads are compensated by the excess resources.

div.head: CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper describes a new method for analyzing the supply and demand bound functions. This paper discusses that it is possible to calculate the overloads that give the system an idea of what is the maximum amount of slack available for recovery. An upper bound on the areas of the demand bound function and a lower bound for the supply bound function are devised. The schedulability test criteria is provided on the overloaded and recovery area. This paper also analyzes the proposed approach of calculating schedulability with regards to the stability requirements of control systems. Simulation results show the metric for overloads for a particular scheduling model, and a case study on double inverted pendulum application validates the schedulability analysis. This analysis can be used to build a compositional embedded real-time control systems because the admission of new tasks can be controlled by analyzing the overloads and its recovery.
